posts.text:
One map, one number, and a 30-year gap in how long you can expect to live depending only on where you're born.

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

a thread 🧵🗺️
1/ The top of the map: Hong Kong and Japan both sit above 84 years, with South Korea close behind. Small, rich, and — not coincidentally — with excellent healthcare access.

2/ The bottom: Nigeria, Chad, the Central African Republic, Lesotho and South Sudan all cluster in the mid-to-high 50s. That's roughly a 30-year gap between the longest- and shortest-lived populations on Earth, in the same year.

3/ It isn't really about old age. It's mostly decided before age 5 — the countries at the pale end of the map are the same ones with the highest child mortality, and losing children young drags the whole average down hard.

4/ Conflict and disease explain much of the rest of southern Africa's gap: Lesotho and its neighbors combine high HIV burdens with, in some cases, recent instability — both of which shorten life expectancy independent of income.
5/ It wasn't always this uneven — or this good. Global average life expectancy was only about 32 years in 1900. It has more than doubled since, but that gain landed very unevenly across the map.

6/ Same species, same century, 30 years of difference depending on the map coordinates you're born into.

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)
